extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, public officials, leaders, and readers interested in public opinion and political organization
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical guidelines about how leaders, symbols, hierarchies (the "machine") and mass opinion interact; useful for evaluating leadership strategy, public persuasion, and institutional organization. Extracts normative/diagnostic criteria on when and why organized leadership and symbolic manipulation succeed or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols are planted by authoritative persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the offering of symbols is generous and their meaning elastic, any particular symbol takes root in a person's mind because it is planted there "by another human being whom we recognize as authoritative" and by people who are "congenial and important."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and elaboration: parents, teachers, and masterful friends introduce symbols in infancy; later we may regard the person who waves the symbol as authoritative. The text emphasizes the social origin of symbolic allegiance rather than spontaneous individual adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: When truth is out of sight, choose trustworthy reporters rather than expect direct verification
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where all the facts are out of sight a true report and a plausible error read alike, sound alike, feel alike. Except on a few subjects where our own knowledge is great, we cannot choose between true and false accounts. So we choose between trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory vs practice: ideally one would choose the most expert, but experts are often indistinguishable, busy, or inaccessible; therefore people rely on identifiable authorities (heads of affairs, newspapers, acquaintances).

rubrics_metrics.name: The necessity of a "machine" (hierarchy) for coordinated action
rubrics_metrics.description: A public without an organized hierarchy cannot construct, devise, negotiate, or administer complex affairs; "by mass action nothing can be constructed, devised, negotiated, or administered." A small number of people present concrete choices to the many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete mechanisms: caucus, nominating convention, steering committee, Council of Ten/Big Three examples; mass action can do Yes/No but cannot exercise sustained administration or complex negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges, incentives and positions (not shared conviction) hold the machine together
rubrics_metrics.description: In a hierarchy "what holds the machine together is a system of privileges" (nepotism, patronage, jobs, publicity, hero-worship, fixed ideas); members' loyalty is structured by superior/subordinate relations rather than identical conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for reform: abolishing particular privileges can disrupt a particular machine, but machines reappear because relative privilege and opportunities will re-crystallize organizational insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols conserve unity by evacuating idiosyncratic ideas into a common emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders cultivate symbols because "in the symbol emotion is discharged at a common target, and the idiosyncrasy of real ideas blotted out." Symbols are focal points where differences merge and therefore useful for mobilizing a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flags, national myths, proto-symbols (nationality); lesser issues are reframed by association with larger symbols (e.g., municipal subway fare becomes 'unAmerican'). Symbols both enable solidarity and simplify complex differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols are instruments of both solidarity and exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because symbols "siphon emotion out of distinct ideas," they enable collective action but also allow a few to "fatten on many, deflect criticism, and seduce men into facing agony for objects they do not understand."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders may be unbelievers in the ideas they propagate yet still use symbols because they work; cautionary note about manipulation and manufactured peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: In crises, secrecy, controlled information, and limited debate can be necessary to preserve unity
rubrics_metrics.description: When quick results are imperative and masses must cooperate in an uncertain environment, manipulation of masses through symbols and withholding public debate may be the only quick way of securing decisive action; "it is usually necessary to secure unity and flexibility without real consent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical illustrations: Foch and Sir Henry Wilson keeping opinions in a small circle in March 1918 to avoid dissolving armies; Captain Wright's account of how publicists paint generals to sustain their command. Paradox: the democratic ideal of publicity is ill-suited to emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must plan policy with regard to morale and the incidence of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every leader must consider not only the merits of a decision but "in its effect on any part of his following whose continued support he requires"; policies with visible, immediate costs are less popular than those with remote or diffuse costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commanders consider troop endurance and casualty lists; politicians prefer indirect taxation, long-term debts, or policies where costs are concealed or postponed. Local issues with visible victims (greedy landlord) provoke action more readily than systemic, remote problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct legislation (initiative/referendum) cannot eliminate the need for leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures like initiative, referendum and direct primary "merely postponed or obscured the need for a machine" because mass decisions must be simplified into a Yes/No form and the choices themselves are created and presented by organized minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ballot realities: measures are often abbreviated; even preferential ballots depend on the quality of choices presented by energetic coteries; the Many vote after the Few nominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: The limit of direct mass action is to say Yes or No to presented issues
rubrics_metrics.description: "The limit of direct action is for all practical purposes the power to say Yes or No on an issue presented to the mass." Masses rarely act fractionally and so require leaders to present concrete choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: unorganized crowds either act in rudimentary, visible ways (strikes, boycotts) or mill about aimlessly; impromptu ringleaders emerge where leadership is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply authorities and provoke expert debate to defend against false premises
rubrics_metrics.description: As "congenital amateurs," individuals' best independence is to multiply the authorities they hear and to 'stir up the experts, and force them to answer any heresy' — this helps detect which arguments stand up in debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation: even this method leaves people vulnerable to false premises that none of the debaters challenge, so it is a defensive rather than infallible strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective leaders first vocalize common feeling then connect their program to it
rubrics_metrics.description: When launching a new policy a leader conducts "a preliminary bid for community of feeling" — vocalizing the prevalent opinion or grievance to gain trust and then setting forth a plan that is verbally/emotionally connected to that feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics: identify with audience by storytelling, patriotism, or pinching a grievance; once trusted, the leader can advance initiatives that may not have been explicitly present in the slogans themselves.
